title: The model in the metal
summary: AMD's agreement to acquire Taalas puts model-specific inference silicon inside a major accelerator roadmap, with enormous vendor-reported efficiency and an equally important loss of flexibility. A large browser game exposes why command approval is a weak agent-security boundary, while Cursor's production router shows how real usage can drive model selection without making satisfaction the same thing as correctness.

threads.name: Custom AI silicon vs Nvidia
threads.status: AMD has agreed to acquire Taalas and says it will integrate the company's model-specific inference technology into its accelerator roadmap while developing system-level solutions alongside Instinct GPUs.
threads.arc: The alternative to Nvidia is broadening from a competing programmable accelerator and software stack into heterogeneous inference, where stable high-volume models may be hard-wired while general GPUs keep the workloads that still change.

dives.story: AMD's agreement to acquire Taalas and bring model-specific silicon into its inference roadmap
dives.why_it_matters: Infrastructure teams deciding what to run on programmable accelerators versus specialized hardware need to understand when a stable, high-volume model can repay the loss of flexibility, and AMD's acquisition makes that trade a mainstream roadmap decision.

dives.story: ScaleX's browser experiment on human approval of coding-agent commands
dives.why_it_matters: Anyone relying on a confirmation prompt as an agent-security boundary needs evidence that people miss quiet scope violations and familiar indirect commands while over-blocking legitimate work.

dives.story: Cursor Router's production-data approach to per-turn model selection
dives.why_it_matters: Engineering teams trying to reduce coding-agent cost need a routing design that prices cache loss and learns task-specific model strengths from real work, while keeping a satisfaction proxy from masquerading as verified correctness.

concepts_taught: model-specific inference silicon: hard-wiring a model's storage and computation to remove the memory-traffic and generality overhead of programmable accelerators, in exchange for checkpoint and architecture flexibility
